specific_author_record.old_source_label: Restoration of the parlements and monarchical legitimacy
specific_author_record.old_target_label: Maupeou reform of 1771
specific_author_record.old_source_meaning: Whole-book synthesis: Louis XVI restored the old courts to signal good intentions, but suppression and restoration had exposed parlementary weakness and royal capacity for despotism, destroying the prior atmosphere of political confidence. The parlements returned amid celebration after Louis XVI's accession but squandered credit through disputes between exiled and collaborating magistrates and through limited resistance after the Turgot episode. The restored courts briefly embodied victory over despotism but lost public authority when they appeared to defend order privilege.
specific_author_record.old_target_meaning: Whole-book synthesis: Maupeou exiled resisting magistrates, abolished parlementary venality, reorganized subordinate courts, and remodeled provincial parlements but failed to secure public legitimacy before Louis XV died. Maupeou's remaking of the parlements provoked nationwide protest; most philosophes saw the loss of intermediary powers as exposure to despotism, while Voltaire supported reform against courts he regarded as obscurantist.

The restored courts briefly embodied victory over despotism but lost public authority when they appeared to defend order privilege.

specific_author_record.old_source_label: Restoration of the parlements and monarchical legitimacy
specific_author_record.old_target_label: Alternatives to despotism
specific_author_record.old_source_meaning: Whole-book synthesis: Louis XVI restored the old courts to signal good intentions, but suppression and restoration had exposed parlementary weakness and royal capacity for despotism, destroying the prior atmosphere of political confidence. The restored courts briefly embodied victory over despotism but lost public authority when they appeared to defend order privilege.

specific_author_record.retained_target_facet: Whole-book synthesis: Louis XVI restored the old courts to signal good intentions, but suppression and restoration had exposed parlementary weakness and royal capacity for despotism, destroying the prior atmosphere of political confidence. The restored courts briefly embodied victory over despotism but lost public authority when they appeared to defend order privilege.
